title: Viola
summary: A computed viola, graded outside the real spread: mostly too dark, attacks far quicker than the recordings, and a noisy band near 395 Hz that is ours, not theirs. Stopped notes sound 11.6 to 19.2 cents sharp of equal temperament (a rigid finger placed at the equal-tempered station, not moved to the note). C3 still plays the old one-oscillator body. Every other note is a string with diameters read from photographs of a playing viola, bowed by a finite-width bow with hair compliance on the friction law measured on real rosin (Woodhouse and Galluzzo 2025), driving a computed shell body (Cassavetti Stradivari outline, 209 modes) and its air cavity at 144 kHz. On D4 and A4 the bow force follows bow speed at the start of the stroke; G3 has its after-length moved off the exact sixth by the cello's printed ratio, borrowed.
physics_present: a computed viola shell body: the outline of the Cassavetti Stradivari viola (Library of Congress), f-holes from its caliper sheet, plate thicknesses from Johannsson's viola table, spruce top and maple back and ribs, a 6.5 mm mesh and all 209 modes its 15 Hz to 5 kHz window holds; the string drives it through bridge flexibility; a 3.24 L air cavity through a physical neck; dry room air; played at 144 kHz on every note but C3
the friction law measured on real rosin (Woodhouse and Galluzzo 2025, eq. 13), on every page including C3

strings with diameters measured on a playing viola (Percival 2013, Table 3.2, from photographs, about 10 %), tension and density from Guettler; the bending stiffness is derived from Percival's measured inharmonicity, because no source prints a viola string's stiffness
a bow of finite width with hair compliance, and bridge and bow flexibility
the after-length (bridge to tailpiece) at one sixth of the speaking length; on G3 it is the sixth times 116/115, the cello's printed ratio, borrowed because no source prints a viola's
stopped notes (E3, C4, Db4, Gb5): a rigid finger on the fingerboard (Issanchou 2017), a 1e13 N/m stop and a 3.5 N press, at its equal-tempered station
on D4 and A4 the bow force follows bow speed through the start of the stroke (Schelleng: both force limits scale with bow speed); the ramp, the final force and the release are unchanged
C3: the older reduced engine, one oscillator for the body radiating as a baffled piston to a listener at 1 m, at 48 kHz, with the measured rosin law
physics_missing: C3 on the shell body: the shell version is refused, because at both 48 and 144 kHz its strongest line sits near 395 Hz and the grader reads it as not the named note (130.8 Hz); the C3 page keeps the stand-in body
the finger moved to the note: stopped notes sound sharp of equal temperament (E3 +12.1 c, Db4 +16.9 c, C4 +19.2 c, Gb5 +11.6 c on the posted pages), where the recordings sit near or below it

what drives a noisy band of lines around the shell's 400.8 Hz pole (strongest near 395 Hz, noise-driven and not a comb, the same place when the note changes) and a fixed line near 200 Hz on the viola pages: neither is explained

the tone and the start of the note: most notes are too dark (D4 centroid 568 Hz against 1210 Hz in the recording) and start far faster than the recordings (D4 attack 104 to 292 ms against 604 ms; C4 18 ms against 342 ms)
harmonics-to-noise as high as the recordings: ours is lower on the pages that state it (C4 14.7 dB against 30.0 dB, Db4 24.3 dB against 33.0 dB)
string loss and bending stiffness from a source: no loss is printed for these strings, so the cards carry none, and the stiffness is derived
blocked: C3 on the shell body stays unposted until a shell render of C3 passes the grader as the named note: the grader refused the shell version as not the named note at both 48 and 144 kHz, its strongest line sitting near 395 Hz.
